newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF, BULGARIA AIM FOR PRUDENT 1997 BUDGET DEFICIT.
newsitem.headline: IMF, BULGARIA AIM FOR PRUDENT 1997 BUDGET DEFICIT.

text.p: Bulgaria needs a prudent 1997 budget deficit to sustain a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime aimed at stabilising the economy, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Wednesday.
"The budget is the bottom line. We are trying to agree on a fiscal deficit that we think is prudent," IMF team leader Anne McGuirk told Reuters.

The IMF mission arrived in Sofia two weeks ago to help prepare introduction of a currency board, a self-regulating mechanism where the lev is pegged to an anchor currency and the amount of levs in circulation must be fully covered by the foreign exchange reserves.
The system bans the central bank from lending to commercial banks and government.

A $657 million reform and funding deal with the IMF envisages reducing budget deficit in 1997 to 3.8 percent from 10.9 percent last year by eliminating the need for central bank credit to the government and rationalising expenditures.
This year's budget is assumed at a lev/dollar exchange rate of 1,600 or 1,000 levs to the German mark, said Finance Minister Muravei Radev on Tuesday.

"I think that we have cleared all issues on structural reform, the main remaining task is to work on the budget and few issues in the banking system," said McGuirk, whose mission is due to end on Friday.
"There are just some final things. We have to agree on the technical assistance programme for banking supervision," she added.
Under the agreement Bulgaria needs to strengthen bank supervision, review all its banking regulations for consistency with international practice and adopt necessary revisions.
The government is also expected to increase capital adequacy requirements to six percent by end-1997 and 10 percent by end-1998, under the deal.
McGuirk said they hoped to complete the work on the budget by Friday. The budget then needs to pass through cabinet and parliamentary approval.
The anchor currency and rate at which it will be fixed will be decided by parliament and announced few days before the currency board system is introduced.
The new reformist government, which took office last week, said the system will be introduced on July 1 and proposed the German mark as anchor currency in the system.

Parliament on Wednesday passed on first, preliminary reading the Banking Bill which sets stricter licensing rules and empowers the central bank to cancel licenses of insolvent banks without right of appeal.
Parliament is expected to debate and pass the Banking Bill and amend the central bank law on second, final reading next week.
The assembly has yet to appoint a new central bank management and a head of its issue department which will play key role in the currency board system.

The IMF will consider disbursing a second tranche of the standby arrangement after the currency board system is in place and Bulgaria has met the reform targets for the first review, said McGuirk. -- Elisaveta Konstantinova, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
